# Benchmark your machine

See how fast AI models run on your computer, and add your results to whatmodel.sh.

## Run it

```sh
curl -fsSL https://whatmodel.sh/bench.sh | sh
```

Needs macOS or Linux (WSL works) with Python 3.9+. Want to read the script before it runs?

```sh
curl -fsSL https://whatmodel.sh/bench.sh -o bench.sh && less bench.sh && sh bench.sh
```

## What happens

1. It looks at your machine and the AI tools you already have.
2. You tick what to test: models you have, models that fit your memory, and your subscriptions. Press `/` to search.
3. It shows exactly what it will run, download and use, then waits for you.
4. Tests run one at a time, in a random order. Ctrl-C stops at any time.
5. Press Enter to upload your results, or upload them later with the command it prints.

Just looking? Try it with pretend models:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://whatmodel.sh/bench.sh | sh -s -- --demo
```

## What's shared

Model names, speeds, runtime versions, and your chip, RAM and OS. Never file paths, prompts, answers, keys or your computer's name. Uploading opens a GitHub issue in your browser with your results filled in, and you press Submit yourself. If they're too long for a link, they're all put on your clipboard to paste in instead. They're released under [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) and checked before they appear.

## Technical details

### What it measures

- **Ollama:** its own timings: generation and prompt tokens/sec, load time, time to the first token (load plus prompt reading) and total time.
- **llama.cpp** (`llama-bench` or `llama bench`) **and MLX** (`mlx_lm.benchmark`): a fixed protocol of a 512-token prompt and the chosen number of generated tokens, one trial per run. They time prompt reading (prefill) and generation separately, so there's no first token or total, and they don't use the gardening prompt.
- **LM Studio and other OpenAI-compatible servers:** a streamed chat reply: first-token time, total time and generation speed from the reported token count. They don't report prefill speed.
- **Reasoning models** count their thinking tokens as generated tokens.
- **Agents** (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI): a fixed short task, its time and tokens. That's not model throughput or coding quality.

Every test gets a warm-up that isn't counted, then shuffled rounds with a random 1-3 s pause before each call. The first second of each pause measures how much CPU other programs are using; the summary warns above 25% and reviewers see it on each result. The run's seed is in the report, so the order and pauses can be replayed. Measurements from different protocols shouldn't be averaged together.

### What it installs or downloads

Only what a ticked test needs, after you start the plan: a runtime's official installer (llama.cpp from llama.app, MLX with `uv tool install mlx-lm`, Ollama's Linux script) and the model download shown in the plan. Desktop apps such as LM Studio open their download page instead. The model list comes from [pages/bench-models.json](pages/bench-models.json), published at `/data/bench-models.json` and generated with the rest of the data.

### The report

It records each result's whatmodel.sh model, runtime, version and quantisation, the per-run numbers, and the machine's OS family, architecture, chip, RAM and GPU. It's saved to `~/.whatmodel/` (readable only by you).

Uploading opens a GitHub issue titled with your machine (for example "Bench results: Mac M2 Pro, 16 GB (6 tests)"): a results table, the machine and method, and the exact report folded away for the maintainers. A link can only carry so much: when the whole issue doesn't fit, none of it goes in the link and all of it is copied to your clipboard to paste, so an issue can't be submitted half-filled. You read it and press Submit; nothing is sent from the script. To upload a saved report later:

```sh
python3 bench.py --upload ~/.whatmodel/bench-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.json
```

### Testing changes

```sh
npm run test:bench
sh -n bench.sh
```

Tests use a loopback fixture and mocked tools, never paid calls or the real GitHub. After changing `bench.py`, update the SHA-256 in `bench.sh`; the tests check they agree. Deploy both files together.
